title: Where Sivers sits in the AI photonics stack
body:
## The layer that doesn't ship to hyperscalers

Investors in Sivers Semiconductors AB sometimes speak as though the company has a direct line into Microsoft's data-centre procurement. It does not. Understanding where Sivers actually sits in the stack — and what that position is worth commercially — is the single most analytically productive exercise in evaluating the company's $453 million pipeline.

The co-packaged optics supply chain runs in layers. At the top sit the hyperscalers: Microsoft, Meta, Amazon Web Services, Google. Below them are the GPU and accelerator vendors — NVIDIA, AMD, Marvell, Broadcom — whose silicon defines the interconnect specifications. Below that is the critical integration layer that the market has only recently begun to scrutinise: the CPO module integrators — POET Technologies, Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, Lightelligence, Celestial AI — whose job is to assemble optical interposers and External Light Source modules compact and efficient enough to sit inside a next-generation AI accelerator package. It is at this layer that the laser question becomes urgent. And it is here, one rung below, that Sivers operates.

Sivers Photonics — the UK-based subsidiary acquired in 2017 as CST Global — manufactures Indium Phosphide DFB lasers and laser arrays. Those components ship not to Microsoft or NVIDIA but to the design houses at the CPO integration layer. Those design houses are the gatekeepers. Whether Sivers' chokepoint position converts to revenue depends entirely on which of its design-house customers wins which hyperscaler design slot — a decision one step outside Sivers' control.

## POET: the most consequential named partnership

On 29 September 2025, Sivers and POET Technologies issued a joint press release announcing a strategic collaboration to develop External Light Source modules for co-packaged optics and the broader AI infrastructure market. The two companies characterised the arrangement as combining Sivers' high-power DFB lasers with POET's Optical Interposer platform — an architecture that embeds III-V light sources into a planar semiconductor structure, replacing discrete fibre connections at the package level.

The commercial logic is straightforward: POET brings the integration substrate; Sivers brings the laser that illuminates it. The target market, per analyst Tim Savageaux, is a $1 billion-plus annual ELS market, sitting inside a broader AI optical connectivity opportunity that multiple parties estimate above $50 billion.

The timeline is tighter than it sounds. Sivers' CEO Vickram Vathulya stated at announcement:

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform."

POET's Executive Chairman and CEO, Dr Suresh Venkatesan, framed the strategic rationale from the integrator's side:

> "Modules optimized for size, performance and cost — exactly what the CPO and AI markets demand."

Early prototypes are targeted for the first half of 2026; production readiness is projected for end of 2026. Both timelines remain to be confirmed by engineering results. POET is a small-cap stock listed on both NASDAQ and the TSX, with its own execution risk. The partnership is real — the product roadmap is aspirational until hardware ships at yield.

## Ayar Labs: the longer, quieter relationship

The Ayar Labs relationship is structurally different from POET's. It predates the current CPO investment cycle and has been demonstrated in public technical forums. At the European Conference on Optical Communications in 2022, Sivers and Ayar jointly showcased DFB laser arrays integrated into Ayar's SuperNova multi-wavelength light source — the optical engine at the centre of Ayar's hyperscale AI interconnect proposition.

The SuperNova is widely regarded as one of the most technically advanced commercial CPO light-source candidates. Ayar Labs, a private company, has disclosed engagement with several hyperscale customers without naming them publicly. Its silicon photonics platform targets in-package optical I/O for AI accelerators — a use case that requires a stable, high-power, thermally consistent C-band light source at the laser foundry level. That is precisely the capability Sivers offers through its Glasgow foundry.

The Ayar relationship matters for two reasons. First, it is a multi-year demonstrated supplier arrangement, not a press-release bilateral. Second, if Ayar wins a design slot with a major hyperscaler, Sivers laser arrays are plausibly inside that win. That indirect exposure is analytically real — it just cannot be stated as a confirmed customer relationship, because Sivers has not confirmed it.

## O-Net/Enablence and the thermal constraint

The third named design-house customer is O-Net Communications, working through its Enablence Technologies subsidiary on ELS modules with integrated thermal solutions for CPO. Thermal management is not a secondary concern in co-packaged optics: laser performance degrades meaningfully with temperature, and the thermal environment inside a tightly integrated GPU package is severe. Yield loss at thermal qualification is one of the primary reasons CPO module production has not yet scaled to hyperscaler procurement volumes.

The O-Net relationship is lower-profile than POET, and O-Net as a mid-cap Chinese company carries its own geopolitical and commercial risks that any investor building a western-supply-chain thesis around Sivers should weigh explicitly.

## imec: the structural endorsement

Before the CPO narrative took hold, Sivers had already established the more technically significant validation that tends to get underweighted in the current hype cycle: a joint development programme with imec — Belgium's microelectronics research consortium and the European reference centre for silicon photonics — that began in 2019. The collaboration integrates C-band InP DFB lasers (operating across the 1,530 to 1,565 nanometre window) onto imec's silicon photonics platform.

imec does not partner casually. Its silicon photonics programme feeds directly into European and US industrialisation programmes for next-generation photonic integrated circuits. A seven-year integration collaboration with imec is a better proxy for the maturity of Sivers' laser technology than any individual commercial press release.

## The wireless and defence customers: a different revenue profile

The photonics stack dominates the AI narrative, but Sivers' wireless segment — housed in Sivers Wireless AB — holds the company's most concretely disclosed revenue commitments. The European Space Agency and Intelsat are named customers for millimetre-wave beamformer hardware used in satellite communications. In May 2026, the US Department of Defense awarded Sivers $6.6 million in Year 2 funding through the Microelectronics Commons programme, supporting domestic defence electronics infrastructure.

The single largest disclosed revenue potential sits with an unnamed automotive LiDAR customer that has committed to deploying Sivers technology "across all their platforms." Analyst estimates for this relationship put the lifecycle revenue at $53 million to $138 million over an eight-to-ten-year period — equivalent to 16 to 44 per cent of FY2025 total revenue of SEK 306.6 million. Production is projected to begin in Q4 2026. Like the CPO partnerships, this remains a forward commitment until the first units ship and are accepted.

## Concentration risk and the pipeline caveat

The $453 million pipeline Sivers disclosed for FY2025 — a 64 per cent year-on-year increase — is distributed across these named partnerships and undisclosed parties. No single customer has been identified as exceeding 25 per cent of that figure. The diversification, on its face, looks like a positive.

The analytical problem is what lies upstream of Sivers. POET is a small-cap company with its own funding pressures. Ayar Labs is private and pre-revenue at hyperscaler scale. O-Net carries cross-border risk. The entire commercial layer that Sivers supplies is itself in early-stage commercialisation. A pipeline distributed across customers who are not yet at scale is not the same as a pipeline distributed across customers who are shipping at volume.

The implied indirect exposure through these design houses — to Marvell (via its 2025 acquisition of Celestial AI), to AMD, to Lightmatter, to Lightelligence — is analytically interesting but should be treated as structural optionality, not as disclosed revenue exposure. Sivers has not confirmed any of these as direct customer relationships.

## The validation test

There is a clean standard for what would confirm the commercial thesis. If NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, or Amazon were to name Sivers — directly or by naming one of its design-house customers in a hyperscale optical-interconnect announcement — the supply-chain position would convert from technically plausible to commercially validated. As of 23 May 2026, none of this has happened.

Sivers' chokepoint is real in a narrow technical sense: there are very few independent western InP DFB laser foundries with the combination of C-band performance, power density, and volume capability that CPO integration demands. The Glasgow facility, inherited from CST Global, occupies a structurally scarce position. But scarcity is a necessary condition for pricing power, not a sufficient one. Whether the chokepoint translates into revenue — and at what margin — depends on decisions being made one layer above Sivers, by companies that are themselves racing to win designs from customers that have not yet committed to CPO at production volumes. The company is the right answer to a question the market is still deciding whether to ask.
